Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Driven magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with CHA based on light-activatable hairpin: A dual-amplification strategy for ultrasensitive hantavirus RNA sensing.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus and poses a potential threat to human health. Current detection methods based on polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays for other hantaviruses such as Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) may carry the risk of false negatives. This study aims to address the technical bottlenecks of low accuracy and insufficient sensitivity in current detection of DBSV. RESULTS: We developed a signal amplification strategy mediated by a photoactivated magnetic 3D DNA walker, which enables light-controllable fluorescence detection. Specifically, this fluorescence sensing platform introduces the catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) technique for dual signal amplification. This system requires dual activation by UV irradiation and target RNA. Then, exonuclease III (Exo III) provides propulsion for the walking process to release a specific trigger strand, subsequently activating the CHA cycle and producing a fluorescent signal. Experimental results confirm that the system displays excellent selectivity and anti-interference ability, successfully distinguishing target sequences with single-base mismatch (SBM), double-base mismatch (DBM), and triple-base mismatch (TBM). Furthermore, the platform achieves a DBSV-RNA detection limit (LOD) of 30 fM with a linear range spanning 10-1-106 pM. The applicability of the method has been rigorously validated using human serum specimens. SIGNIFICANCE: This study provides a novel strategy for the application of spatiotemporally controllable DNA walkers in RNA detection, demonstrating considerable potential for early viral diagnosis and field monitoring.

analysis.background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may pose a threat to human health.
analysis.methods: A photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker coupled with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) was engineered; activation requires UV irradiation and target RNA, and exonuclease III drives the walker to release a trigger strand that initiates CHA, with validation using human serum specimens.
analysis.results: The platform displayed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM for DBSV RNA with a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM, and performed reliably in serum samples.
analysis.contribution: The dual‑amplification, spatiotemporally controllable DNA‑walker strategy provides a novel tool for early hantavirus diagnosis and field monitoring.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed experimental conditions, sample size, and field performance are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantavirus dabieshanense (DBSV) is a newly emerging hantavirus that may threaten human health. Methods: A photo‑activated magnetic 3D DNA walker combined with catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) was created, requiring UV light and target RNA, with exonuclease III propulsion, and validated on human serum specimens. Results: The system showed excellent selectivity, distinguishing single‑, double‑ and triple‑base mismatches, achieved a detection limit of 30 fM and a linear range of 10⁻¹–10⁶ pM, and worked well in serum. Contribution: This spatiotemporally controllable dual‑amplification approach offers a promising tool for early hantavirus diagnosis and field monitoring. Limitations: Only the abstract is provided; detailed methods, sample size, and broader performance data are not reported.

papers.title: In Silico Prediction and Structural Mapping of Linear B-Cell Epitopes in Andes Virus Glycoprotein as Potential Vaccine Candidates
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. This study aimed to identify and structurally map linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein using an immunoinformatics-based approach. The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt, and linear B-cell epitopes were predicted using BepiPred 3.0 with a threshold of 0.030. Candidate peptides were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Five preliminary epitope candidates were identified, among which E1, E2, E3, and E4 met the antigenicity criterion. The refined structure showed favorable validation parameters, with an ERRAT score of 97.73 and 97.88% of residues in the favored Ramachandran region. Structural mapping indicated that E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) were positioned on exposed surface regions, supporting their prioritization as the most promising candidates. E4 (PSTSSTDT) also showed potential, whereas E3 (HPRGEDHD), despite having the highest antigenicity score, appeared less structurally exposed. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates in ANDV glycoprotein. However, experimental validation is required to confirm their immunological relevance.

Royhan Afnani1,3, Muhammad Fajrul Adi Syahputra1, Rangga Adhi Prastika2,3, Abdul Rahman Siregar1* 1Department of Biology, Faculty of Biology, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, 55281, Indonesia 2Department of Nanotechnology Engineering, Faculty of Advanced Technology and Multidiscipline, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya 60115, Indonesia. 3Drug and Vaccine Innovation Research Group, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Surabaya, Indonesia *Corresponding author: ar.siregar@ugm.ac.id ARTICLE HISTORY Received: 16 Jun 2026 Revised: 21 Jul 2026 Accepted: 29 Jul 2026 Published: 30 Sep 2026 ABSTRACT Andes virus (ANDV), a pathogenic orthohantavirus associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, remains a public health concern because of its severe clinical outcomes and the absence of broadly approved vaccines for human use. The viral glycoprotein is a relevant antigenic target because of its surface localization and role in viral entry. Candidate peptides were evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1, and ToxinPred, respectively. The three-dimensional glycoprotein model was generated using AlphaFold, refined with GalaxyWEB, and validated using ERRAT and Ramachandran plot analysis. Surface-localized candidates were further assessed through molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure using ClusPro 2.0, followed by binding free energy estimation using PRODIGY. E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE), E2 (QTKTVNLRGT), and E4 (PSTSSTDT) showed favorable antigenicity, non-allergenic and non-toxic profiles, and surface localization on the glycoprotein model. Docking analysis further supported their prioritization, with predicted binding free energies of -10.0, -9.4, and -9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2, and E4, respectively. Overall, E1 emerged as the strongest candidate, while E2 and E4 represent additional candidates for further validation. These findings provide preliminary computational evidence for candidate linear B-cell epitopes in ANDV glycoprotein, although experimental confirmation remains necessary. Keywords: Andes virus; B-cell epitope; glycoprotein; immunoinformatics; structural mapping; candidate linear B-cell epitope Introduction A recent cluster of Andes virus infections associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius has heightened international concern regarding the public health significance of pathogenic orthohantaviruses (Koopmans et al., 2026). Andes virus (ANDV), a zoonotic pathogen within the genus Orthohantavirus and family Hantaviridae, typically infects humans through inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodent reservoirs. Notably, ANDV is epidemiologically unique due to documented instances of limited person-to- person transmission, particularly among close contacts (Chediack et al., 2026; Martinez- Valdebenito et al., 2014). This transmission feature, combined with its association with severe cardiopulmonary disease, underscores the importance of ANDV for public health surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and vaccine development. ANDV is a primary etiological agent of hantavirus Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), a severe disease marked by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, acute respiratory failure, and cardiogenic shock (Warner et al., 2025). While the incidence of HCPS is generally lower than that of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by Old World hantaviruses, HCPS exhibits a substantially higher case-fatality rate, typically reported at 30–40% (Angulo et al., 2017; Barrera et al., 2025; Quarleri et al., 2026). Despite the clinical severity of ANDV infection, no specific antiviral therapy or widely approved vaccine is currently available for human use. This lack of medical countermeasures is particularly concerning given ecological disturbances, climate variability, and habitat changes that may influence rodent population dynamics and elevate the risk of human exposure to infected reservoirs (Moirano et al., 2024). Structurally, ANDV is an enveloped, negative- sense RNA virus with a tripartite genome consisting of small, medium, and large segments. The small segment encodes the nucleocapsid protein, the medium segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into Gn and Gc, and the large segment encodes the RNA- dependent RNA polymerase (Beltrán-Ortiz et al., 2017). The envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc are of particular interest for vaccine development because they are displayed on the virion surface and mediate host-cell attachment, receptor engagement, endocytic entry, and membrane fusion. Their surface exposure facilitates antibody recognition, supporting their selection as antigenic targets for epitope-based vaccine research (Banerjee & Mukhopadhyay, 2016; Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014). B-cell epitopes are specific antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and contribute to humoral immune responses (Caoili, 2022). In vaccine design, identifying B-cell epitopes is essential because antibody-mediated immunity and immunological memory are critical for protection against viral reinfection. Linear B-cell epitopes are particularly valuable in immunoinformatics-based screening, as they can be derived from the primary amino acid sequence, assessed for antigenicity and safety, and mapped onto three-dimensional antigen structures (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). However, sequence-based prediction alone does not adequately determine biological accessibility or immunogenic potential. Structural mapping is therefore required to establish whether predicted epitopes are located on solvent-exposed regions of the target protein, where they are more likely to be accessible to antibody binding (Afnani & Purnama, 2025; Francino-Urdaniz & Whitehead, 2021). Although B-cell epitope prediction, multiepitope vaccine design, and structural evaluation have been applied in viral vaccine- related studies, including hantavirus targets, most previous hantavirus immunoinformatics studies have emphasized broad whole-proteome screening or multiepitope vaccine construct design rather than a focused prioritization of linear B-cell epitopes derived specifically from the ANDV glycoprotein (Abdulla et al., 2021). The novelty of the present study therefore does not rely on the use of individual computational tools, which are well-established in immunoinformatics research, but on the ANDV- specific integration of linear B-cell epitope prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure for candidate prioritization. This integrated approach allows predicted epitopes to be evaluated not only on the basis of sequence-level epitope propensity, but also according to their predicted antigenicity, safety profile, structural localization, and interaction potential with an antigen-recognition model. Such a focused framework is particularly relevant for glycoprotein antigens, in which not all sequence- predicted epitopes are necessarily exposed or available for antibody recognition on the folded protein surface. Therefore, this study aimed to identify and prioritize linear B-cell epitope candidates in the Andes virus glycoprotein through an integrated immunoinformatics approach combining sequence-based prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure. Candidate epitopes were further assessed for antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, structural localization, and predicted BCR-binding affinity. The results provide preliminary computational evidence for prioritized surface-accessible linear B-cell epitope candidates that may inform future experimental evaluation for Andes virus vaccine-associated or diagnostic applications. However, as this study is Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya entirely computational, the predicted epitopes should be regarded as potential candidates requiring further experimental validation through in vitro and in vivo studies. Materials and Methods Retrieval and Curation of Andes Virus Glycoprotein Sequence The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from the UniProt Knowledgebase using the taxonomic identifier and protein accession as search criteria. The UniProt entry Q9E006, annotated as ANDV glycoprotein and consisting of 1138 amino acids, was selected as the reference sequence for downstream analysis (Shimizu et al., 2013). The FASTA sequence and associated metadata, including accession number, organism name, protein length, and database source, were recorded to ensure sequence traceability and reproducibility. UniProtKB provides curated protein sequence and functional annotation resources, supporting its use as a primary source for protein sequence retrieval. Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction Linear B-cell epitope prediction was performed using BepiPred 3.0, a sequence-based epitope prediction tool developed for identifying residues with potential B-cell epitope propensity (Clifford et al., 2022). The higher-confidence prediction option was selected. In this study, a threshold of ≥0.030 was used as a sequence-specific operational cutoff based on the score distribution observed across the ANDV glycoprotein. This cutoff was selected to balance epitope recovery and prediction stringency. Higher cutoff values retained only a very limited number of short epitope regions and reduced the ability to capture biologically plausible contiguous peptide segments, whereas lower cutoff values increased the inclusion of low-scoring regions that may represent less reliable predictions. Antigenicity, Allergenicity, and Toxicity Screening The predicted linear B-cell epitope candidates were further evaluated for antigenicity, allergenicity, and toxicity. Antigenicity was assessed using VaxiJen v2.0 with a threshold value of 0.400; peptides with antigenicity scores above this threshold were considered potentially antigenic (Afnani, Kharisma, et al., 2026). VaxiJen is an alignment-independent antigen prediction server that classifies antigens based on the physicochemical properties of protein sequences (Doytchinova & Flower, 2007). Allergenicity was predicted using AllerTOP v2.1, and only peptides classified as non-allergenic were retained. AllerTOP is an alignment-free allergenicity prediction server based on physicochemical properties and machine-learning classification (Dimitrov et al., 2014). Toxicity was evaluated using ToxinPred, and peptides predicted as non-toxic were prioritized for further structural mapping. ToxinPred is designed to classify peptides as toxic or non-toxic based on computational sequence-derived features (Rathore et al., 2024). Prediction, Refinement, and 3D Structure Validation The three-dimensional (3D) structure of the Andes virus glycoprotein was predicted using the AlphaFold Server (Kovalevskiy et al., 2024; Prastika et al., 2026). The predicted structure was then refined using the GalaxyWEB server to improve local structural geometry and reduce potential modeling artifacts. The refined model was validated using structure quality assessment parameters (Ko et al., 2012). The ERRAT score was calculated using the Structure Validation Server, and stereochemical quality was assessed using Ramachandran plot analysis through RamPlot (Afnani, Emilia, et al., 2026; Laskowski et al., 2013). The validated model was subsequently used as the structural template for mapping the selected linear B-cell epitope candidates. Structural Mapping and Visualization of Linear B-Cell Epitope Candidates The selected linear B-cell epitope candidates were mapped onto the refined 3D structure of the ANDV glycoprotein using PyMOL under an academic license. Epitope positions were identified based on their amino acid coordinates in the full-length glycoprotein sequence and visualized on the 3D model using distinct colors. Both cartoon and surface representations were generated to assess the spatial distribution and surface exposure of each candidate epitope (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Epitope candidates located on surface-exposed regions were prioritized because B-cell epitopes are more likely to be accessible to antibody recognition when positioned on the external surface of the antigen. In contrast, epitopes located within Journal of Tropical One Health Volume 1 (2026) Nariswari et al. h/ps://doi.org/10.22452/jtoh.vol1.1 Published by Tropical Infec5ous Disease Research and Educa5on Centre (TIDREC), Universi5 Malaya buried, transmembrane, or structurally uncertain regions were interpreted with caution and were not prioritized for further analysis. Molecular Docking with B-Cell ReceptorThe prioritized linear B-cell epitopes, were further evaluated through molecular docking with the B- cell receptor (BCR). The BCR structure was obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank using PDB ID 5IFH (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). Molecular docking was performed using the ClusPro 2.0, with BCR designated as the receptor and each epitope peptide as the ligand (Arapa et al., 2026). The best-ranked docking complex from each epitope-BCR interaction was selected for further evaluation. The predicted binding free energy (ΔG) of each complex was then assessed using the PRODIGY web server, where more negative ΔG values indicate stronger predicted binding affinity (Xue et al., 2016). The resulting docking complexes were visualized using PyMOL to examine the interaction orientation and spatial positioning of each epitope on the BCR surface. This analysis is significant because B-cell epitopes represent antigenic regions recognized by antibodies and may serve as preliminary targets for vaccine- associated evaluation, immunodiagnostic development, and immune-reactivity assessment. Linear B-cell epitopes are particularly valuable in immunoinformatics-based screening, as they can be derived from the primary amino acid sequence, assessed for antigenicity and safety, and mapped onto three-dimensional antigen structures (Riswana & Punjungsari, 2025). However, sequence-based prediction alone does not adequately determine biological accessibility or immunogenic potential. Structural mapping is therefore required to establish whether predicted epitopes are located on solvent-exposed regions of the target protein, where they are more likely to be accessible to antibody binding (Afnani & Purnama, 2025; Francino-Urdaniz & Whitehead, 2021). Although B-cell epitope prediction, multiepitope vaccine design, and structural evaluation have been applied in viral vaccine- related studies, including hantavirus targets, most previous hantavirus immunoinformatics studies have emphasized broad whole-proteome screening or multiepitope vaccine construct design rather than a focused prioritization of linear B-cell epitopes derived specifically from the ANDV glycoprotein (Abdulla et al., 2021). The novelty of the present study therefore does not rely on the use of individual computational tools, which are well-established in immunoinformatics research, but on the ANDV- specific integration of linear B-cell epitope prediction, antigenicity and safety screening, three-dimensional structural mapping, and molecular docking with a B-cell receptor structure for candidate prioritization. This integrated approach allows predicted epitopes to be evaluated not only on the basis of sequence-level epitope propensity, but also according to their predicted antigenicity, safety profile, structural localization, and interaction potential with an antigen-recognition model. Such a focused framework is particularly relevant for glycoprotein antigens, in which not all sequence- predicted epitopes are necessarily exposed or available for antibody recognition on the folded protein surface. analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with severe outcomes and no broadly approved human vaccine, representing a public‑health concern.
analysis.methods: The ANDV glycoprotein sequence was retrieved from UniProt and linear B‑cell epitopes were predicted with BepiPred 3.0 (threshold 0.030); candidate peptides were screened for antigenicity, allergenicity and toxicity using VaxiJen v2.0, AllerTOP v2.1 and ToxinPred; a 3‑D glycoprotein model was built with AlphaFold, refined by GalaxyWEB and validated (ERRAT, Ramachandran); surface‑exposed candidates were further docked to a B‑cell receptor using ClusPro 2.0 with binding free energies estimated by PRODIGY.
analysis.results: Five preliminary epitopes were identified, of which E1, E2, E3 and E4 met antigenicity criteria; the refined model showed an ERRAT score of 97.73 % and 97.88 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions; structural mapping placed E1 (EWRKKSDTTDTTNAASTTFE) and E2 (QTKTVNLRGT) on exposed surfaces, while E3 was less exposed; docking yielded predicted binding free energies of –10.0, –9.4 and –9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2 and E4 respectively, highlighting E1 as the strongest candidate.
analysis.contribution: The study provides preliminary computational evidence of surface‑accessible linear B‑cell epitopes in the ANDV glycoprotein, offering candidate targets for future epitope‑based vaccine design.
analysis.limitations: All findings are based on in‑silico predictions; experimental validation of antigenicity, immunogenicity and protective efficacy is required.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes severe cardiopulmonary syndrome and lacks approved vaccines, posing a public‑health threat. Methods: The glycoprotein sequence was retrieved, linear B‑cell epitopes predicted with BepiPred 3.0, screened for antigenicity, allergenicity and toxicity, modeled in 3‑D with AlphaFold, refined and validated, and surface candidates docked to a B‑cell receptor. Results: Five epitopes were found, four met antigenicity; E1 and E2 were surface‑exposed, with docking free energies of –10.0, –9.4 and –9.1 kcal/mol for E1, E2, E4, and the model showed high validation scores. Contribution: Provides computationally identified epitope candidates for ANDV vaccine research. Limitations: Findings are purely computational and need experimental confirmation.

papers.title: Transmisión interpersonal del virus Andes: revisión narrativa de la evidencia actual y sus implicaciones clínicas
papers.abstract: Los hantavirus constituyen un grupo de virus responsables de zoonosis emergentes transmitidas principalmente por roedores. El virus Andes (ANDV), endémico de Sudamérica, constituye una excepción dentro de este grupo viral debido a la evidencia de transmisión interpersonal limitada. El objetivo de esta revisión narrativa es actualizar la evidencia disponible sobre la transmisión humano-humano del ANDV y analizar sus implicaciones clínicas y epidemiológicas. Se realizó una búsqueda bibliográfica narrativa en PubMed/MEDLINE y Google Scholar, incluyendo estudios epidemiológicos, revisiones y trabajos experimentales relevantes. Los brotes descritos en Argentina y Chile, junto con estudios moleculares y modelos animales, apoyan la existencia de transmisión interpersonal en contextos de contacto estrecho y prolongado, especialmente durante fases iniciales de la enfermedad. La detección de ARN viral en saliva y secreciones respiratorias aporta plausibilidad biológica a este fenómeno. La capacidad de transmisión interpersonal del ANDV posee implicaciones relevantes para el aislamiento, el rastreo de contactos y la vigilancia epidemiológica en áreas endémicas. Hantaviruses constitute a group of viruses responsible for emerging zoonotic diseases primarily transmitted by rodents. Andes virus (ANDV), endemic to South America, is unique among hantaviruses because of evidence supporting limited person-to-person transmission. The aim of this narrative review is to summarize current evidence regarding interpersonal transmission of ANDV and its clinical and epidemiological implications. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar including epidemiological studies, reviews, and experimental reports. Outbreaks described in Argentina and Chile, together with molecular studies and animal models, support the existence of person-to-person transmission in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly during the early stages of disease. Detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions provides biological plausibility for this phenomenon. The transmissibility of ANDV has relevant implications for patient isolation, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance in endemic regions.

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 引起新出现的动物源性疾病,主要通过啮齿动物传播;安第斯病毒(ANDV)在 汉坦病毒es 中独特,因为已有报告显示有限的人际传播。
analysis_zh.methods: 在 PubMed/MEDLINE 和 Google Scholar 中进行叙述性文献检索,纳入流行病学研究、综述和实验报告。
analysis_zh.results: 阿根廷和智利的暴发事件,结合分子研究和动物模型数据,支持在密切、长期接触的环境中,尤其是疾病早期,ANDV 的人际传播;在唾液和呼吸道分泌物中检测到病毒 RNA,提供了生物学可行性。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该证据为安第斯病毒在流行地区的隔离措施、接触者追踪和流行病学监测提供依据。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒es 引起新出现的动物源性疾病,主要通过啮齿动物传播;安第斯病毒(ANDV)在 汉坦病毒es 中独特,因为已有报告显示有限的人际传播。 方法：在 PubMed/MEDLINE 和 Google Scholar 中进行叙述性文献检索,纳入流行病学研究、综述和实验报告。 结果：阿根廷和智利的暴发事件,结合分子研究和动物模型数据,支持在密切、长期接触的环境中,尤其是疾病早期,ANDV 的人际传播;在唾液和呼吸道分泌物中… 贡献：该证据为安第斯病毒在流行地区的隔离措施、接触者追踪和流行病学监测提供依据。 局限：仅提供摘要,未报告详细数据、研究质量评估和定量估计。

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses
papers.abstract: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898.

Black 37 Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower 38 apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing 39 particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 40 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc 41 complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for 42 efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1- 43 directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly 44 reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. 45 Importance 46 The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely 47 characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we 48 show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses 49 associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for 50 efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two 51 viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that 52 PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes 53 from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents 54 infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, 55 emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody 56 neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein 57 surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown. 58 59 Introduction 60 Entry of enveloped viruses into host cells is a major determinant of tissue tropism and 61 cross-species transmission(1). Mammalian hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae, order 62 Elliovirales) are emerging zoonotic pathogens that cause severe, often fatal illness in 63 humans after transmission from chronically infected small-mammal reservoirs, 64 manifesting as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and 65 hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in the Americas (2, 3). The public health 66 significance of hantaviruses is underscored by their recurring emergence, including a 67 multi-country HCPS outbreak in April-May 2026, which involved limited secondary 68 transmission and resulted in three reported deaths (4–6). Despite significant morbidity 69 and high case-fatality rates approaching 40% for HCPS, no FDA-approved 70 prophylactics or antiviral therapeutics are currently available (7). Cellular entry of 71 hantaviruses is orchestrated entirely by the envelope glycoprotein complex Gn/Gc (8, 72 9). Gn and Gc are synthesized as a single polyprotein precursor encoded by the 73 medium (M) genomic segment, co-translationally cleaved by cellular signal peptidases, 74 and assemble into spike-like tetramers of Gn/Gc heterodimers on the virion envelope 75 (8–11)These glycoproteins coordinate entry: the membrane-distal Gn subunit likely 76 mediates host receptor engagement, while the class II fusion protein Gc drives low-pH- 77 dependent membrane fusion within late endosomes envelope (8–12) Despite the 78 identification of dozens of hantavirus species across rodent and insectivore hosts 79 globally, host entry receptors and neutralization vulnerabilities for most divergent 80 species remain undefined (10, 13, 14). 81 Candidate hantavirus attachment factors and receptors initially identified through 82 antibody blockade, ligand competition, or in vitro binding assays include β1, β2, and β3 83 integrins, decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55), and gC1qR complement receptor (15– 84 19). However, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss-of-function screens in human 85 microvascular endothelial cells, a primary in vivo target cell type, demonstrated that 86 knockout of ITGB1, ITGB3, or DAF had little or no effect on infection by a panel of 87 virulent hantaviruses, indicating that these molecules are dispensable for endothelial 88 cell entry (20). Point mutations within the EC1 contact surface disrupt 94 infection, establishing PCDH1-EC1 as the functional interface (22). Although PCDH1 95 usage has been established for multiple hantaviruses, the glycoprotein determinants 96 that govern receptor recognition across divergent lineages remain incompletely defined 97 (20–22). PCDH1 usage has also been documented beyond the canonical New World 98 clade, including in vole- and mole-borne viruses (23), but its distribution across other 99 rodent- and shrew-borne clades has yet to be fully mapped. 100 Gn/Gc amino acid sequences differ by roughly 40-60% between hantavirus lineages, 101 and most glycoprotein-directed monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) raised or isolated against 102 one species show little heterologous neutralization (24, 25). Consequently, broadly 103 active entry inhibitors may need to target either conserved virus-receptor interfaces or 104 rare, functionally constrained epitopes on the viral spike (11, 21, 24, 25). On the host 105 side, the EC1-specific mAb-3305, soluble histidine-tagged PCDH1 ectodomain proteins 106 containing EC1-2 or EC1-4 (sEC1-2, sEC1-4), and a human Fc-tagged soluble EC1 107 decoy (EC1-Fc) block PCDH1-Gn/Gc engagement and neutralize PCDH1-dependent 108 viruses (21–23). Conversely, targeting conserved epitopes on the viral spike can 109 provide broad neutralization across clades. In particular, mAb-42898, isolated from a 110 Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus puumalaense)-convalescent individual, binds a 111 quaternary epitope bridging the Gn capping loop and Gc fusion loops, neutralizes 112 multiple HCPS- and HFRS-causing viruses, and protects rodents against lethal 113 challenge (24, 26). This 129 panel includes viruses with distinct and incompletely defined zoonotic relevance. TIGV 130 circulates in peridomestic rodents in Ethiopia, where orthohantavirus-reactive antibodies 131 were detected in human sera (35). DBSV is genetically related to the prototypic HFRS- 132 causing Hantaan virus (HTNV), whereas CBNV and MGAV are shrew-borne viruses 133 with no established association with human disease (13, 29). 134 BCCV and LANV are particularly notable because authentic isolates exist for both, and 135 each has been studied extensively in epidemiologic, reservoir, and animal-model 136 settings. Here we show that all six Gn/Gc 145 complexes mediate infection of human microvascular endothelial cells, consistent with 146 systematic pseudotype screens showing that receptor-binding proteins from diverse 147 animal viruses can function broadly in human cells (1). CRISPR/Cas9-based genetic 148 depletion and cDNA complementation in human cells demonstrated that infection 149 mediated by glycoproteins of BCCV and LANV—but not those of DBSV, TIGV, CBNV, 150 or MGAV—depends on PCDH1. Concordantly, BCCV and LANV glycoproteins bound 151 soluble PCDH1 with different efficiencies in sEC1-2 capture ELISAs, were competitively 152 blocked at this interface by EC1-specific mAb-3305, and were neutralized by EC1-Fc 153 and mAb-3305 in endothelial cell infection assays. The panel 164 included the New World rodent-borne viruses Black Creek Canal virus (BCCV) and 165 Laguna Negra virus (LANV), the Old World rodent-borne viruses Dabieshan virus 166 (DBSV) and Tigray virus (TIGV), and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus (CBNV) and 167 Amga virus (MGAV) (Fig. 1A). An enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) 174 reporter was included in the first transcriptional unit to permit quantitation of infected 175 cells (Fig. 1B, top). Consistent with established rVSV rescue strategies for Old World 176 rodent-borne, mole-, and shrew-borne viruses, constructs from DBSV, CBNV, TIGV, 177 and MGAV contained the Hantaan virus (HTNV)-derived rescue-enhancing substitutions 178 I532K in the Gn cytoplasmic tail and S1094L in the membrane-proximal stem of Gc 179 ectodomain (23, 41) (Fig. 1B bottom). In selected constructs, adjacent residues were 180 also replaced with their HTNV counterparts. These modifications promote plasma- 181 membrane localization and rVSV incorporation of HTNV Gn/Gc and lie outside the 182 receptor-binding interface and the mapped neutralizing-antibody epitopes evaluated 183 here. 184 Recovery of rVSV-BCCV required an S430C substitution. Because cysteine is highly 185 conserved at the corresponding position among mammalian hantaviruses, the serine 186 reported in the deposited BCCV GenBank sequence may reflect a sequencing error 187 rather than authentic viral variation. In contrast, 224 PCDH1 status had little or no effect on infection by rVSV-DBSV, rVSV-CBNV, rVSV- 225 TIGV, and rVSV-MGAV, paralleling the well-established PCDH1-independent infection 226 of rVSV-HTNV. 227 We confirmed this phenotype in TIME cells, providing an endothelial cell context 228 relevant to hantavirus tropism. analysis.methods: Replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes were used to assess entry in primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells and human osteosarcoma cells (A2, F8‑F10).
analysis.results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected endothelial cells with varying efficiencies; genetic ablation of protocadherin‑1 (PCDH1) markedly reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, while re‑expression restored susceptibility (A3‑A4). Methods: Replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes were used to assess entry in primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells and human osteosarcoma cells. Results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected endothelial cells with varying efficiencies; genetic ablation of protocadherin‑1 (PCDH1) markedly reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, while re‑expression restored susceptibility. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc incorporated less glycoprotein and showed lower PCDH1 capture than Laguna Negra and Andes virus, yet PCDH1 depletion did not affect the other four hantaviruses. All six viruses were potently neutralized by a broadly reactive Gn/Gc antibody. papers.title_zh: Laguna Negra 与 Black Creek Canal 病毒对 PCDH1 的差异性利用 汉坦病毒es

analysis_zh.background: Laguna Negra 病毒和 Black Creek Canal 病毒是与 汉坦病毒心肺综合征 相关的 汉坦病毒,但其细胞进入受体尚不清楚 (A1, F16‐F18)。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用携带 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 复合体的可复制重组水疱性口炎病毒评估其在原代人肺微血管内皮细胞和人骨肉瘤细胞中的进入情况 (A2, F8‐F10)。
analysis_zh.results: 所有六种 Gn/Gc 复合体均能感染内皮细胞,感染效率各异;基因敲除 protocadherin‐1 (PCDH1) 显著降低了 Laguna Negra 和 Black Creek Canal 病毒的感染,而重新表达则恢复了易感性 (A3‐A4)。可溶性 PCDH1 细胞外结构域可捕获两种病毒,且使用诱饵或 EC1 特异性抗体可抑制感染,表明 EC1 介导了结合 (A5‐A6)。Black Creek Canal 的 Gn/Gc 蛋白掺入的糖蛋白较少,且 PCDH1 捕获水平低于 Laguna Negra 和 安第斯病毒,但 PCDH1 缺失对其他四种 汉坦病毒 无影响 (A7‐A8)。所有六种病毒均被一种广谱 Gn/Gc 抗体强效中和 (A9)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,Laguna Negra 和 Black Creek Canal 汉坦病毒 通过 PCDH1 实现高效进入,但在受体结合方式和抑制剂敏感性上存在差异,凸显近缘病毒的异质性;同时显示广谱中和抗体能够针对多种 汉坦病毒 (A4‐A6, A9, F15‐F20)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Vaccines for the prevention of hantavirus fevers: An overview of results and development prospects
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION. Hantavirus fevers, known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with a wide range of clinical manifestations. The causative agents are members of the genus Orthohantavirus , whose natural reservoirs are rodents of various species. There is currently no etiotropic therapy for these diseases. Specific prophylaxis through vaccination is available only in the DPRK, the Republic of Korea, and the People's Republic of China. An important objective is to provide the Russian and European markets with a relevant vaccine for HFRS prevention. Such a vaccine should be developed based on both time-proven approaches and the experience of modern developments. AIM. Analysis of the use of existing hantavirus vaccines and the specific features of vaccines under development, as well as assessment of the prospects for creating vaccines for HFRS prevention in the Russian Federation. DISCUSSION. All commercially available vaccine preparations are inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on the Hantaan and Seoul viruses. The effectiveness of these preparations varies, but a significant reduction in the incidence rate in regions with mass vaccination and a low incidence of adverse events have been noted. Several inactivated whole-virion vaccines based on relevant orthohantavirus strains have been developed in Russia. Some of these developments have successfully completed preclinical studies. The spectrum of hantavirus vaccine preparations under development includes subunit vaccines, vaccines based on virus-like particles (VLPs) and viral vectors, DNA vaccines, and mRNA vaccines. The primary immunogens are the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc of hantaviruses. The closest to implementation into clinical practice are the DNA vaccines based on the Puumala and Hantaan viruses, which have undergone clinical trials (phase I). CONCLUSIONS. No vaccine for the prevention of hantavirus infections developed using virus-like particles (VLPs), viral vectors, or nucleic acids (DNA or mRNA) has undergone a full cycle of clinical trials or been licensed worldwide. On the contrary, well-established traditional technologies for manufacturing inactivated vaccines and their time-proven effectiveness provide a basis for their real prospects of practical application in the Russian Federation and other European countries.

papers.full_text: Вакцины для профилактики хантавирусных лихорадок: обзор результатов и перспектив разработок https://doi.org/10.30895/2221-996X-2026-26-3-324-335 Резюме ВВЕДЕНИЕ. Хантавирусные лихорадки, регистрируемые как геморрагическая лихорадка с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) на Евроазиатском и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС) на Американском континентах, представляют собой природно-очаговые болезни с широким диапазоном клинических проявлений. Возбудители — представители рода Orthohantavirus, резервуаром которых в природе являются грызуны различных видов. Этиотропной терапии хантавирусных лихорадок в настоящее время не существует. Специфическая профилактика в форме вакцинации проводится только в КНДР, Республике Корее и КНР. Важной задачей является обеспечение российского и европейского рынка актуальной вакциной для профилактики ГЛПС. Противохантавирусная вакцина должна разрабатываться как с учетом подходов, доказавших временем свою эффективность, так и опыта современных разработок. ЦЕЛЬ. Анализ применения существующих хантавирусных и особенностей разрабатываемых вакцин, а также оценка перспектив создания вакцин для профилактики ГЛПС в Российской Федерации. ОБСУЖДЕНИЕ. Все коммерчески доступные вакцинные препараты являются инактивированными цельновирионными вакцинами на основе вирусов Хантаан и Сеул. Эффективность этих препаратов различается, но отмечается существенное снижение заболеваемости в регионах с массовой вакцинацией и низкая частота побочных явлений. В России разработаны несколько инактивированных цельновирионных вакцин на основе актуальных штаммов ортохантавирусов. Некоторые из разработок успешно прошли доклинические испытания. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. full_text_sections.full_text: Вакцины для профилактики хантавирусных лихорадок: обзор результатов и перспектив разработок https://doi.org/10.30895/2221-996X-2026-26-3-324-335 Резюме ВВЕДЕНИЕ. Хантавирусные лихорадки, регистрируемые как геморрагическая лихорадка с почечным синдромом (ГЛПС) на Евроазиатском и хантавирусный пульмональный синдром (ХПС) на Американском континентах, представляют собой природно-очаговые болезни с широким диапазоном клинических проявлений. Возбудители — представители рода Orthohantavirus, резервуаром которых в природе являются грызуны различных видов. Этиотропной терапии хантавирусных лихорадок в настоящее время не существует. Специфическая профилактика в форме вакцинации проводится только в КНДР, Республике Корее и КНР. Важной задачей является обеспечение российского и европейского рынка актуальной вакциной для профилактики ГЛПС. Противохантавирусная вакцина должна разрабатываться как с учетом подходов, доказавших временем свою эффективность, так и опыта современных разработок. ЦЕЛЬ. Анализ применения существующих хантавирусных и особенностей разрабатываемых вакцин, а также оценка перспектив создания вакцин для профилактики ГЛПС в Российской Федерации. ОБСУЖДЕНИЕ. Все коммерчески доступные вакцинные препараты являются инактивированными цельновирионными вакцинами на основе вирусов Хантаан и Сеул. Эффективность этих препаратов различается, но отмечается существенное снижение заболеваемости в регионах с массовой вакцинацией и низкая частота побочных явлений. В России разработаны несколько инактивированных цельновирионных вакцин на основе актуальных штаммов ортохантавирусов. Некоторые из разработок успешно прошли доклинические испытания. Спектр разрабатываемых хантавирусных вакцинных препаратов представлен субъединичными вакцинами, вакцинами на основе вирусоподобных частиц и вирусных векторов, ДНК- и мРНК-вакцин. В качестве основных иммуногенов используются поверхностные гликопротеины Gn и Gc хантавирусов. Наиболее близко к внедрению в медицинскую практику оказались ДНК-вакцины на основе вирусов Пуумала и Хантаан, прошедшие клинические исследования (фаза I). ЗАКЛЮЧЕНИЕ. Ни один вакцинный препарат для профилактики хантавирусных инфекций, разработанный на основе вирусоподобных частиц, вирусных векторов, нуклеиновых кислот, не прошел полного цикла клинических испытаний и не лицензирован в мире. Напротив, отлаженные традиционные технологии изготовления инактивированных вакцин и их доказанная временем эффективность обусловливают реальные перспективы их практического применения в России и других европейских странах. analysis.background: Hantavirus fevers, known as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the Americas, are natural focal diseases with a wide range of clinical manifestations.
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Vaccination is currently practiced only in the DPRK, South Korea, and China; inactivated whole‑virion vaccines have shown a significant reduction in incidence in regions with mass vaccination and low adverse‑event rates; DNA vaccines based on Puumala and Hantaan viruses have reached phase I clinical trials; no VLP, viral‑vector, DNA or mRNA vaccine has completed a full clinical trial cycle or been licensed worldwide; traditional inactivated vaccine technologies are viewed as the most realistic option for implementation in Russia and other European countries.
analysis.contribution: The paper outlines the objective of providing a Russian/European HFRS vaccine, analyses existing vaccines and those under development, and emphasizes the practical prospects of traditional inactivated vaccines while noting emerging platforms.
analysis.limitations: The article is an overview without original experimental data; quantitative efficacy figures are not presented; conclusions rely on previously reported information rather than new research.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus fevers (HFRS in Eurasia, HPS in the Americas) are natural focal diseases with diverse clinical manifestations. Methods: not reported in the supplied evidence. Results: Vaccination is only used in DPRK, South Korea, and China; inactivated whole‑virion vaccines reduce incidence in mass‑vaccination areas with few adverse events; DNA vaccines for Puumala and Hantaan have reached phase I trials; no VLP, viral‑vector, DNA or mRNA vaccine has completed full trials or been licensed; traditional inactivated vaccines are seen as most feasible for Russia and Europe. Contribution: The review identifies the need for a Russian/European HFRS vaccine, evaluates existing and pipeline products, and highlights the prospects of traditional inactivated vaccines alongside newer platforms. Limitations: The paper provides only an overview, lacks original data and quantitative efficacy details, and bases conclusions on existing literature.

papers.title_zh: 用于预防汉坦病毒热的疫苗:结果概述与发展前景

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒热,在欧亚地区称为肾综合征出血热,在美洲称为汉坦病毒肺综合征,是自然灶性疾病,临床表现范围广泛。
analysis_zh.methods: 未在提供的证据中报告。
analysis_zh.results: 目前疫苗接种仅在DPRK、韩国和中国开展;灭活全病毒疫苗在大规模接种地区显示出显著降低发病率且不良事件率低;基于普马拉病毒和汉滩病毒es的DNA疫苗已进入I期临床试验;全球尚无VLP、病毒载体、DNA或mRNA疫苗完成完整临床试验周期或获批上市;传统灭活疫苗技术被视为在俄罗斯及其他欧洲国家实施的最现实方案。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本文阐明提供俄欧肾综合征出血热(HFRS)疫苗的目标,分析现有疫苗及在研疫苗,并强调传统灭活疫苗的实际前景,同时指出新兴平台的出现。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本文为综述性文章,未提供原始实验数据;未呈现定量疗效数值;结论基于已有报道而非新研究。

papers.title: Climate change as an amplifier of hantavirus risk in South Asia: a neglected nexus.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is seroepidemiologically established in South Asian human populations and rodent reservoirs, with anti-hantavirus antibodies confirmed in occupational risk groups in India, an independent association with chronic kidney disease demonstrated in Sri Lanka, and co-infection with leptospirosis identified in more than one-fifth of hospitalized leptospirosis patients. Despite this, the intersection of these findings with the region's intensifying monsoon floods, rapid urbanization, and climate-driven rodent ecology remains entirely unexamined. This letter highlights the neglected climate-hantavirus nexus, identifies structural vulnerabilities that amplify transmission risk in South Asia, and calls for integrated flood-response surveillance and One Health coordination across the region.
papers.journal: Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

papers.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

source_records.title: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning

papers.full_text: A noetic fractal-fractional dynamical formalism for history-dependent Seoul virus–Streptococcus pyogenes dual-pathogen interaction with physics-informed learning Abstract Seoul virus is an important rodent-borne hantavirus that can cause serious illness in humans, while Streptococcus pyogenes is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen associated with a wide range of infections and severe complications. The interaction between these two infections is not well understood from a mathematical modeling perspective. In this work, we develop a fractal–fractional model to investigate the transmission and co-infection dynamics of Seoul virus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The model is described using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo fractal–fractional derivative so that the effects of memory and the nonuniform nature of disease transmission can be represented more realistically than in conventional integer-order models. Several mathematical properties of the proposed system are studied, including the existence and uniqueness of solutions and the behavior of the disease-free equilibrium. The basic reproduction number is obtained to identify the threshold conditions associated with the spread of the infections, and the Ulam–Hyers stability of the model is also examined. In addition to the theoretical analysis, a physics-informed neural network is constructed to approximate the solutions of the fractal–fractional system. The governing equations and initial conditions are incorporated into the neural-network training process, allowing the model structure to guide the numerical approximation. The simulations illustrate the influence of the fractional and fractal parameters on the evolution of the co-infection system and show that the PINN approach can reproduce the model dynamics with good accuracy. The findings suggest that combining fractal–fractional operators with physics-informed learning offers a useful way to study co-infectious disease systems in which memory, heterogeneity, and nonlinear interactions play an important role. analysis.background: Seoul virus is an important rodent‑borne hantavirus that can cause serious illness in humans, and Streptococcus pyogenes is a clinically significant bacterial pathogen; the interaction between these two infections is not well understood from a mathematical modeling perspective.
analysis.methods: The authors develop a fractal‑fractional model of co‑infection using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative to capture memory and heterogeneity, analyze existence, uniqueness, disease‑free equilibrium and the basic reproduction number, and construct a physics‑informed neural network that incorporates the governing equations and initial conditions for numerical solution.

analysis.contribution: The study shows that integrating fractal‑fractional operators with physics‑informed learning offers a useful framework for investigating memory‑dependent, heterogeneous co‑infectious disease systems.
analysis.limitations: Only abstract and partial text are provided; no empirical data, validation, or detailed methodological specifics are reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Seoul virus is a rodent‑borne hantavirus causing serious illness and Streptococcus pyogenes is a major bacterial pathogen; their co‑infection dynamics lack mathematical description. Methods: A fractal‑fractional model using the Atangana–Baleanu–Caputo derivative was built, with theoretical analysis of solutions, equilibrium and reproduction number, and a physics‑informed neural network incorporated governing equations for numerical approximation. Results: Unique solutions, disease‑free equilibrium, a basic reproduction number and Ulam–Hyers stability were derived; simulations indicated fractional and fractal parameters affect dynamics and the PINN reproduces them accurately. Contribution: Combining fractal‑fractional operators with physics‑informed learning provides a novel tool for studying memory‑dependent co‑infectious disease systems. Limitations: Only abstract and partial text are available; no empirical validation is reported.
